senses.gloss: c. (b. h.; preced.) way, road; method, manner.
units: Kidd. 2ᵇ ד׳ לשון וכ׳ derekh is feminine gender &c.
<cite ref="Kiddushin 2b:13">Ib.</cite> <he>דַרְכּוֹ של אישׁ וכ׳</he> it is man’s way to carry war, and not woman’s.—
<cite ref="Jerusalem Talmud Nedarim 1:1:5">Y. Ned. I, beg. 36ᶜ</cite>, a. e. <he>התורה דיברה כדַרְכָּהּ</he>, v. <cite ref="L00705"><he>לָשׁוֹן</he></cite>.
<cite ref="Mishnah Sukkah 2:1">Succ. II, 1</cite> <he>לפי דַרְכֵּינוּ</he> by our way (incidentally).

<cite ref="Avodah Zarah 15b:13">Ab. Zar. 15ᵇ</cite> <he>כד׳ שאסור</he> … <he>כך וכ׳</he> Ms. M. (ed. <he>כד׳ שאמרו אסור</he>) on the same principle that &c.; a. v. fr.—<he>דֶּ׳ אֶרֶץ</he> (abbrev. <he>ד״א</he>) the way of the land,
<cite ref="Pirkei Avot 2:2">Ab. II, 2</cite> study <he>עם ד״א</he> combined with a trade.
<cite ref="Tosefta Sotah 7:20">Tosef. Sot. VII, 20</cite> <he>לימדה … ד״א וכ׳</he> the Torah teaches incidentally the proper conduct that one must first build a house &c.—
<cite ref="Gittin 70a:24">Gitt. 70ᵃ</cite> bot. <he>ד׳ וד״א וכ׳</he> travelling, marital connection &c.
<cite ref="Bereishit Rabbah 22:6">Ib.</cite> s. 80 <he>כדַרְכָּהּ</he> natural gratification of sexual appetite, <he>שלא כד׳</he> unnatural. Ib. s. 18, end; a. fr.—
<cite ref="Sanhedrin 31b:17">Snh. 31ᵇ</cite> <he>העביר עלי את הד׳</he> mutilated me (oth. interpret.: wronged me in business).—Pl. <he>דְּרָכִים</he>.

<cite ref="Rosh Hashanah 17a:4">R. Hash. 17ᵃ</cite> <he>פירשו מדַּרְכֵי ציבור</he> they deviated from the ways of the community, became heretics.—<he>דרכי אמורי</he>, v. <cite ref="A02007"><he>אֱמוֹרִי</he></cite>.—<he>דרכי שלום</he> ways of peace (ref. to <cite ref="Proverbs 3:17">Prov. III, 17</cite>); <he>מפני ד׳ ש׳</he> because the ways of the Law are ways of peace (differ. fr. <he>משים איבה</he>, v. <cite ref="A01120"><he>אֵיבָה</he></cite>), i.e. it is a demand of equity, good manners &c., though no special law can be quoted for it.
Gitt. V, 8 sq.; a. fr.—(ד״א) דרך ארץ Derekh Erets (Manners), name of a treatise attached to Talmud editions, divided into Rabba (Large), and Zuta (Small).
